question: What makes a good friend?
html:
A good friend is someone who wishes you well for your own sake and stays steady, and the friendship lasts when both people keep giving the sentiment rather than just receiving it.

Start with what you want for the other person. A friend wants good things for their friend's sake, not for what they get back, and wants them to stay the person they are.

I mean, people define a friend to be “one who intends and does what is good (or what he believes to be good) to another for that other’s sake,” or “one who wishes his friend to be and to live for that friend’s own sake” (which is the feeling of mothers towards their children, and of friends who have come into collision).

Aristotle, The Nicomachean Ethics, Chapter IV, para. 1

If then it has been rightly said that a friend wishes to his friend good things for that friend’s sake, it must be understood that he is to remain such as he now is: that is to say, he will wish the greatest good to him of which as man he is capable: yet perhaps not all, because each man desires good for himself most of all.

Aristotle, The Nicomachean Ethics, Chapter VIII, para. 9

Notice that this care for a friend grows out of how you treat yourself. If you are at odds with yourself, you have little to give. The person who is unified and wants their own good is the one who can genuinely wish it for another.

Now the friendly feelings which are exhibited towards our friends, and by which Friendships are characterised, seem to have sprung out of those which we entertain toward ourselves.

Aristotle, The Nicomachean Ethics, Chapter IV, para. 1

(For, as has been said before, goodness, that is the good man, seems to be a measure to every one else.) For he is at unity in himself, and with every part of his soul he desires the same objects; and he wishes for himself both what is, and what he believes to be, good; and he does it (it being characteristic of the good man to work at what is good), and for the sake of himself, inasmuch as he does it for the sake of his Intellectual Principle which is generally thought to be a man’s Self.

Aristotle, The Nicomachean Ethics, Chapter IV, para. 1

Friendship lives in the giving, not the getting. Those who are fond of their friends are the ones praised, and when that feeling is present in the right measure, the friendship holds.

Since then Friendship stands rather in the entertaining, than in being the object of, the sentiment, and they are praised who are fond of their friends, it seems that entertaining the sentiment is the Excellence of friends; and so, in whomsoever this exists in due proportion these are stable friends and their Friendship is permanent.

Aristotle, The Nicomachean Ethics, Chapter VIII, para. 11

Envy has no place here. Clear it out so that the good things your friend has feel like your own, and what you have feels like theirs.

And as to envy they will make a clean sweep and clearance of it: the good things which a man possesses shall be also the property of his friends, and the goods which they possess are to be looked upon as his.

Xenophon, The Memorabilia, BOOK II, para. 168

Give the other person room. Treat your friend with reverence and as something to behold rather than something to hold close. Their merits are not yours, and they need space to grow and expand.

Treat your friend as a spectacle.

Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays, p. 132

Reverence is a great part of it.

Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays, p. 132

Of course he has merits that are not yours, and that you cannot honor, if you must needs hold him close to your person. Stand aside; give those merits room; let them mount and expand.

Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays, p. 132
